newsitem.title: USA: Outlook good for US cane refiners--USDA aide says.
newsitem.headline: Outlook good for US cane refiners--USDA aide says.

text.p: The future looks sweet for U.S. sugar cane refiners, despite their fears about losing market share to beet processors and their complaints about U.S. sugar policy, a U.S. Agriculture Department aide said Monday.

During the first six months of 1997, refined cane sugar prices averaged 6.46 cents per pound above raw sugar prices, compared to an average margin of 3.86 cents in 1992-96, USDA sugar program adminstrator Robert Barry said.

"While margins vary, cane refining--relative to sugar beet processing--is expected to hold its own over the 7-year course of the 1996 Farm Act," Barry said in comments prepared for the American Sugar Alliance's annual meeting here.
Until relatively recently, the U.S. Cane Sugar Refiner's Association was part of the ASA along with groups representing sugar growers and sugar beet and sugar cane processors.

However, the cane refiners broke with the rest of the industry and joined the Sweeteners User Association in criticizing the U.S. sugar program, which keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels. Congress reformed the sugar
program in the 1996 farm bill, but it maintained an annual import quota restricting the amount of raw cane sugar allowed into the United States.
Cane refiners fear that quota gives sugar beet processors an edge in meeting future U.S. refined sugar demand. But such concern "does not appear to be warranted," Barry said.

U.S. beet processors are projected to supply 44 to 45 percent of domestic demand through the end of the farm bill in the year 2002, virtually unchanged from about 44 to 46 percent over the past 5 years, Barry said.

If anything, the 1996 farm bill has improved prospects for sugar cane refiners. Without the reforms in that legislation, USDA projected the beet share of domestic refined sugar "deliveries" to rise 48 to 49 percent, Barry said.

Rep. Tom Ewing, an Illinois Republican and chairman of the House Agriculture subcommittee on specialty crops and risk management, told ASA members he did not expect significant changes in the sugar program over the next couple of years.
"I am confident that we will be able to overcome any of the battles that lie ahead," Ewing said.
Last month, the latest effort to change the sugar program failed by 78 votes in the U.S. House.
In addition, 67 percent of new House members voted to keep the program in its current form, Ewing said.
Given that large victory, "it is my sincere hope that the annual legislative attacks on the program will cease," he said.
